2) For embeddings + reranker: how do you recommend batching vs freshness trade-offs? What are typical vector sizes and latency for your embedding models?
3) Structured output/tool calling: how robust is function-calling to guarantee parsable JSON (we need to avoid repeated parsing errors in prod)?
4) Chat vs completions: for streaming responses, how are stop sequences handled and what does partial JSON look like when streaming? Also concerned about tokenization differences across models (we use token accounting for cost forecasting).

From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
To: Samira Khan <samira.khan@acmeco.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 26 Mar 2026 11:08:00 -0700
Subject: RE: ACME - SDK & integration follow-up (auth, routing, schema questions)

Hi Samira — great talking earlier. I put together concise answers and sample request/response snippets below. I also attached the SDK sample (redwood-sdk-sample-requests.md) with runnable cURL and Python examples. High-level first, then concrete behaviours you asked about.

1) Auth:
- Recommended: token-exchange flow (your short-lived JWT -> Redwood short-lived token). This avoids long-lived API keys and lets you map ACME user/tenant metadata into Redwood for auditing and rate limits.
- Private deployment: supports mTLS for service endpoints and local token validation; for hybrid setups we support routing rules so high-sensitivity requests can be routed to your private cluster while lower-sensitivity go to hosted.
- Implementation notes: we expose a /token-exchange endpoint (customer calls with internal JWT, we validate via your introspection endpoint or signed JWT) and return a short-lived ephemeral token (1-15m TTL) which the SDK uses for subsequent calls. We can also support OAuth client-credentials for service-to-service in dedicated setups.

2) SDK setup & request patterns (chat vs completions):
- Chat payload (JSON shape): {"model": "rwd-chat-1", "messages": [{"role":"system","content":"..."}, {"role":"user","content":"..."}], "max_tokens": 512, "temperature":0.2, "stream": true}  
- Completions payload (JSON shape): {"model": "rwd-complete-1", "prompt": "...", "max_tokens": 256, "stop": ["\n\n"], "stream": true}
- Key differences: chat uses an ordered messages array with roles (system, user, assistant). Completions use a single prompt string. For context window accounting both use tokenizer-based token counts; chat may add role/meta tokens.

3) Tokenization / billing semantics:
- We tokenize using a consistent BPE tokenizer per model family. Billing is per input+output token. For chat endpoints we count tokens for the entire messages array plus generated tokens. For cost forecasting: provide sample prompts and we'll run a tokenization dry-run to surface typical token counts.

4) max_tokens / stop sequences:
- max_tokens caps the number of tokens generated in the response. If you set max_tokens too low the model may truncate.
- stop accepts one or more sequences. When using streaming, stop sequences are honored server-side: streaming will finish once a stop sequence is emitted, but the exact final delimiter may appear as the last chunk or as part of the final chunk depending on chunk boundaries. We recommend implementing a small client-side post-processing check for stop tokens on the final assembled string.

5) Streaming semantics and partial JSON (structured output / function calling):
- Streaming sends delta tokens as they are generated. For structured outputs we support two modes: 
  a) function-calling / structured output mode: the model emits a structured payload (e.g., a JSON object) in the assistant or function object. The SDK will provide a higher-level helper that accumulates tokens and emits a final parsed JSON object when complete. If streaming partial JSON (e.g., for large arrays) the client should buffer tokens and only attempt to parse on end-of-stream or receipt of a close signal.
  b) tagged JSON blocks: if you prefer non-streaming predictable output, set stream=false and we will return fully-formed JSON in the response body; this is best for strict parsers.
- Edge cases: if the model produces malformed JSON mid-stream (rare), the SDK helper will expose raw token stream + a final parsing error to let you decide (retry vs fallback). We also support a post-processing / validation hook to enforce schemas and automatically retry with a higher temperature=0 and system prompt nudges if parse fails.

6) Embeddings & reranker recommendations: 
- Model/size: for semantic search we typically recommend rwd-embed-512 (512-d vectors) for general semantic similarity; for domain/large-context you may prefer rwd-embed-1536.
- Batching: small batches (up to 64) tend to give best latency/throughput trade-offs for CPU/GPUs; we support both synchronous single-call embedding and an async bulk ingest API for large backfills.
- Reranker pattern: compute embeddings for candidate docs and the query, then use a lightweight dot-product or cosine similarity stage to shortlist, then run a fast reranker model (completions or compact chat) on the top N for fine-grained scoring. For freshness, keep embeddings for newly-added docs in a nearline queue and batch every 30–120s depending on your freshness SLA.

7) Routing & fallbacks:
- You can configure routing rules by request metadata (tenant, sensitivity flag) to route to hosted vs private clusters. We also support automated fallback to a lower-cost model variant if capacity is constrained.

8) Samples & SDK helpers:
- Attached sample file (redwood-sdk-sample-requests.md) includes: cURL + Python chat streaming example, completions sample with stop sequences, tokenization dry-run commands, and an embeddings ingestion snippet with batching and retry strategies.

If helpful, I can paste short sample request/response snippets inline in the meeting so you can copy/paste. Otherwise I can add them to the Drive doc before the call.

Pls confirm the meeting time and I'll send an invite + a short agenda.

Cheers,
